title: The Grand Expedition: the four-terrain traverse
summary: They cross the whole map in ten climbs, six for what the desert taught and one old friend from each season of the arc, perform the twelve coins with real coins and a balance, retell the root 2 proof in two minutes, and then take the examiner's chair and grade the grown-ups at the whiteboard.
materials: the Field Atlas, open at the coverage ledger, and a pen that will still be readable in ten years
twelve matching coins and the two-pan balance, on a table where the room can see both pans
the field journal, open at the root 2 pages
the whiteboard and markers, for grading the grown-ups in front of them
five problems from four seasons, chosen by you and printed, one copy per grown-up
pencil, paper and graph paper for the traverse
the four wall maps, forest, coast, mountains and desert, up together for the first time

steps.title: How the traverse runs
steps.body:
Today nobody examines you. You run the day, and this is the hour you built the rest of it around.

The traverse is ten climbs and it crosses the whole map. Six come from what the desert taught: two statistics climbs on your own logged data, two counting climbs and one chance climb from the last province of the book, and the smallest criminal, sprint 3's one tool. The other four are old friends, one from each terrain. What never changes, from the forest. The binary balance, from the coast. Assume the opposite, from the mountains. And the mirage, from here.

They are climbs, not a test. Nothing is timed, paper is allowed on every one of them, and a climb you have to fight your way up counts exactly the same as one you walk.

Afterwards, three things happen at the table, and they are the reason the Atlas is open.

First the coverage ledger. Every chapter of the book gets one line: which week you crossed it, which climb witnessed it, and which page of the journal holds the working. You sign it yourself. A stranger has to be able to read that page without you standing beside them explaining it, so write it for the stranger.

Second, the claim, read out loud with its witnesses on the table. Entering grade 5, ready for Algebra 1, and here is what stands behind it. Witness one is this ledger, and it stands on its own. If the family settled on a readiness check, and you sat it quietly in an ordinary week, that is witness two. Read out what it actually said, whatever it said. It was never a grade and it does not turn into one today. If there was no check, say that plainly and read the ledger alone. A claim with one honest witness beats a claim with two when one of them was invented.

Third, the honest arithmetic, said in your own voice, because a claim that rounds itself up is a mirage like any other. The target was three grade levels ahead by the end of grade 5, which is June 2028. You are saying it now, most of a school year before that date. Say it that way. The smaller true sentence is worth more than the bigger one, and everybody in the room can tell the difference.

problems.prompt: Climb 1, the statistics you ran on your own four seasons of logs. Six Build hours from one sprint, minutes actually spent: 55, 58, 60, 62, 65 and 180. Which single number describes a typical Build hour honestly?
options: The mean, 80 minutes, because it uses every reading in the list.
The median, 61 minutes, because one very long morning sits far above the rest and pulls the mean above five of the six readings.
The mode, because the length that happens most often is the most typical one.
The range, 125 minutes, because it reaches from the shortest hour to the longest.
explanation: Sorted, the middle pair is 60 and 62, so the median is 61 minutes. The six total 480, so the mean is 80 minutes.
Five of the six mornings ran under 66 minutes, well below a mean of 80.
The 180 is the morning the compiler fought back. It drags the mean and hardly moves the median at all.
The mode is a trap: nothing here repeats.
problems.useAgain: when one reading sits far away from the rest and somebody wants a single number for what is typical.
hints: Work out both middles before you choose between them. Which one changes if you delete the 180?
Sort the six numbers and take the middle pair for the median, then add all six and divide by six for the mean.
problems.socraticHint: If you told somebody a typical Build hour was 80 minutes, how many of your six mornings would that sentence describe?

variant.prompt: Seven recordings, in minutes: 8, 9, 9, 10, 11, 12 and 13. Which single number describes a typical recording honestly?
options: The median, 10 minutes, because the readings sit close together and nothing runs away from the pack.
The mode, 9 minutes, because 9 is the only length that happens twice.
The range, 5 minutes, because it reaches from the shortest to the longest.
None of them, because the mean of this list is not a whole number.

problems.prompt: Climb 2, and the log tells the truth about its own holes. Your dawn log has a line for each of 84 mornings. Nine lines are blank because you were away. The 75 readings you did write add up to 1,350 degrees. What is the mean of the mornings you actually recorded?
explanation: A mean divides a total by how many things made the total, and only 75 mornings put anything into this one.
1,350 divided by 75 is 18 degrees.
Dividing by 84 instead gives about 16.1, which quietly invents nine freezing dawns you never recorded.
An honest report says the number and the hole together: 18 degrees, over 75 mornings out of 84 recorded.
problems.useAgain: when a log has gaps in it and somebody wants one number out of the whole thing.
hints: Nine mornings carry no reading at all. Did they put anything into the 1,350?
Divide the total by how many readings actually exist, and say that count out loud beside your answer.
problems.socraticHint: What would you be quietly claiming about those nine blank mornings if you divided by 84?

variant.prompt: The app logged 40 sessions this season, but the timer was off for 6 of them. The 34 sessions that do carry minutes add up to 1,326. What is the mean of the sessions you actually recorded?

problems.prompt: Climb 3, counting the opposite. You toss a coin six times and write the run down as a row of heads and tails. There are 64 possible rows. How many of them contain at least two heads?
explanation: At least two heads is five jobs in one. Its opposite is tiny: no heads at all, or exactly one.
One row has no heads. Six rows have exactly one, because that single head can sit in any of the six places.
That is 7 rows in the opposite camp, so 64 take away 7 leaves 57.
problems.useAgain: when the thing you are counting says at least, and the leftovers are a much shorter list than the thing itself.
hints: Counting the rows with two, three, four, five and six heads is five separate jobs. How many jobs is the opposite?
Count the rows that fail the condition, then take that off 64.
problems.socraticHint: Which is the shorter list to write out here, the rows you want or the rows you do not?

variant.prompt: You toss a coin five times, which gives 32 possible rows. How many of them contain at least two tails?

problems.prompt: Climb 4, every pair counted twice. Twelve people come to the Expedition and everybody shakes hands with everybody else, except that the four who arrived together as one family greeted each other in the car and skip the handshakes inside their own group. How many handshakes happen?
explanation: If everybody shook everybody, each of the 12 shakes 11 hands, which counts 132 hands. Every handshake got counted from both ends, so halve it to 66.
The same count inside the family of four: 4 times 3 is 12, halved to 6 handshakes that never happen.
66 take away 6 is 60.
problems.useAgain: when everybody in a group pairs with everybody else and your count walked outwards from each person.
hints: Count the handshakes first as if nobody skipped anything at all.
The skipped handshakes are their own smaller everybody-with-everybody problem, on 4 people.
problems.socraticHint: When you count outwards from each person in turn, how many times does one single handshake get written down?

variant.prompt: Ten people are in the room and everybody shakes hands with everybody else, except that the three who live in the same house skip the shakes among themselves. How many handshakes happen?

problems.prompt: Climb 5, the chance of a small thing. Twelve coins sit in a bag and exactly one of them is the fake. You reach in without looking and take out three coins. What is the probability that the fake is one of the three?
explanation: Look at it from the fake coin's own side. Every coin in the bag is equally likely to be picked.
Three of the twelve come out, so the fake's chance of being one of them is 3 out of 12, which is 1/4.
The long count agrees: of the 220 ways to choose three coins, 55 hold the fake.
problems.useAgain: when one marked thing sits in a pile and you want the chance it lands in the handful you take.
hints: You do not have to count handfuls at all. Ask what happens to one particular coin.
Every coin is equally likely to be chosen. How many of the twelve get chosen?
problems.socraticHint: Is the fake coin any more or less likely to be picked than the ordinary coin lying next to it?

variant.prompt: Ten name slips go into a hat and one of them is yours. Three slips are drawn out. What is the probability that yours is one of them?

problems.prompt: Climb 6, sprint 3's one tool. The claim is that every whole number bigger than 1 is a product of primes. Suppose the claim fails somewhere, and let N be the smallest number bigger than 1 that fails. Which step arrests N?
options: N must be even, so 2 is one of its prime factors and the claim holds for N after all.
N minus 1 is smaller than N, so N minus 1 is a product of primes, and adding 1 keeps it one.

N is not prime, so N is a times b with both factors bigger than 1 and smaller than N. Both sit below the smallest failure, so both are products of primes, and their prime lists joined together build N.
N is the smallest failure, so nothing smaller than N is allowed to be looked at.
explanation: N cannot be prime, since a prime is its own product of primes. So N is a times b, with both pieces between 1 and N.
Both sit below the smallest failure, so neither fails, and each is a product of primes.
Joining their prime lists builds N from primes, so N never failed either.
The N minus 1 option is the trap: adding 1 wrecks a number's factors entirely.
problems.useAgain: when a claim is about every whole number and one failure can be turned into a smaller failure.
hints: The method needs a smaller version of the same crime. Where would a smaller number come from here?
Write down what being the smallest failure guarantees: every number from 2 up to N minus 1 obeys the claim. Now find a way to spend that.
problems.socraticHint: Why does calling N the smallest failure hand you free information about every number underneath it?

variant.prompt: The claim is that every whole number bigger than 1 has at least one prime factor. Let N be the smallest number bigger than 1 with no prime factor at all. Which step arrests N?
options: N is odd, so 3 must divide it.
N minus 1 has a prime factor, and any factor of N minus 1 is also a factor of N.
N is the smallest failure, so every factor of N is bigger than N is.
N is not prime, so it has a factor d with d bigger than 1 and smaller than N. That d sits below the smallest failure, so d has a prime factor, and that prime divides N as well.

problems.prompt: Climb 7, an old friend from the forest: the thing that never changes. A token starts on the bottom left square of a 5 by 5 grid. Each step moves it to a square sharing an edge with the one it is on, and in 24 steps it visits all 25 squares, each exactly once. True or false: it can finish on the top right square.
explanation: Colour the grid like a chessboard with the bottom left dark. Every step swaps colour, so the path alternates all the way.
A 5 by 5 grid has 13 dark squares and 12 light, corners included. So a 25 square path starting dark must end dark.

The top right corner is dark, so nothing is broken and a snake up the rows does it. Change the size of the board and the two counts change with it, so run the colouring again rather than trusting this answer.
problems.useAgain: when a move alternates between two kinds of place and you want to know where it is allowed to stop.
hints: Colour the squares like a chessboard before you try to draw a single path.
Count the dark squares and the light squares, then ask what colour the 25th square has to be.
problems.socraticHint: If every single step swaps the colour under the token, what decides the colour of the square it lands on last?

variant.prompt: A token starts on the bottom left square of a 4 by 4 grid, and in 15 steps it visits all 16 squares, each exactly once, always stepping to a square sharing an edge. True or false: it can finish on the top right square.

problems.prompt: Climb 8, an old friend from the coast: the balance written in binary. Three piles hold 3, 5 and 9 stones. Players take turns, a move takes any number of stones from one single pile, and whoever takes the last stone wins. You move first, and there is exactly one winning first move. How many stones does it take?
explanation: Stack the piles in binary, with 3 as 11, 5 as 101 and 9 as 1001 underneath.
Pair the powers off column by column. Eights, fours, twos and ones all come out odd, so this position is unbalanced.
Balancing means every column pairs off, and only the 9 can manage it. It has to fall to 6, since 3, 5 and 6 balance.
9 take away 6 is 3 stones.
problems.useAgain: when a take-away game has several piles at once and you want the move that hands the loss to the other player.
hints: Three piles cannot be judged by size alone. Write them in binary and stack them one under another.
A balanced position has an even count in every binary column. Find which single pile can be lowered until that is true.
problems.socraticHint: Could more than one of the three piles be the one you move in, and how would you know that before trying them all?

variant.prompt: Three piles hold 4, 7 and 9 stones, same rules again, and again there is exactly one winning first move. How many stones does it take?

problems.prompt: Climb 9, an old friend from the mountains, spending what you proved this season. You know that root 2 cannot be written as a fraction of two whole numbers. True or false: 1 plus root 2 can be written as a fraction of two whole numbers.
explanation: Assume the opposite. Suppose 1 plus root 2 equals p over q, with p and q whole numbers.
Take 1 off both sides. Root 2 becomes p minus q, over q, and both of those are whole numbers.
That makes root 2 a fraction of whole numbers, which you proved is impossible. The assumption is the only thing left that can be wrong.
problems.useAgain: when you already know one number escapes fractions and somebody hands you a close relative of it.
hints: Do not start on root 2. Start by supposing the whole thing is a fraction and see what falls out of it.
Subtracting 1 from a fraction of whole numbers leaves a fraction of whole numbers.
problems.socraticHint: What could you do to that supposed fraction to leave root 2 sitting on its own on one side?

variant.prompt: You know that root 2 cannot be written as a fraction of two whole numbers. True or false: root 2 multiplied by root 2 can be written as a fraction of two whole numbers.

problems.prompt: Climb 10, and the desert's own idea. Somebody hands you a rule: n times n, plus n, plus 41, is prime for every whole number n starting at 0. You test n = 0, 1, 2 and 3 and it holds. A friend tests every n up to 39 and it still holds. What is the smallest n where the rule fails?
explanation: Surviving more tests is what a mirage does. Forty passing checks are not a proof, so look at the shape instead.
n times n, plus n, is just n times the next number up. So the whole thing is n times (n plus 1), with 41 added on.

Whenever n or n plus 1 is a multiple of 41, so is the answer. But when n is 0 the answer is 41 itself, which is prime. The rule first really fails when n is 40, where the answer is 41 times 41, or 1,681, not a prime.
problems.useAgain: when a rule has passed every test you threw at it and you still have not looked at why it would be true.
hints: More passing tests do not make a rule true. Ask instead what could put a factor of 41 into the answer.
Rewrite n times n, plus n, as a single product, then hunt for the n that drops a factor of 41 into it.
problems.socraticHint: If the rule really were true, what would the reason be? And if you cannot find a reason, what have all those passing tests actually shown you?

variant.prompt: Somebody hands you a rule: n times n, plus n, plus 17, is prime for every whole number n starting at 0. It holds for every n up to 15. What is the smallest n where the rule fails?

steps.title: The twelve coins, performed, and the monsters by name
steps.body:
The month 3 monster gets its performance. Twelve coins on the table, one balance, and an audience.

Set it up so the room can see both pans. Hand the coins to somebody, turn your back, and let them choose which coin is the odd one and whether it is heavy or light. They write it down and say nothing else the whole way through.

Then run it out loud. Say what you are about to weigh and why before each weighing rather than after it, because the reason is the whole interesting part and afterwards it just sounds like luck. Three weighings, then name the coin and say which kind of odd it is.

Nothing on this page tells you which coins to put where. The scheme is yours, out of your own week with it, and if you have to stop and restart a weighing in front of everybody, that is a better thing for a room to watch than a smooth performance of somebody else's plan.

Then the half that makes it mathematics rather than a trick. Say out loud why three weighings can carry enough information and two never can. Do the counting where they can see it: count the answers you are trying to tell apart, remembering that each coin comes in two flavours of wrong, then count what a single weighing can possibly tell you, remembering that a balance has three things it can do and not two. Put those two counts side by side and let the room watch them meet.

Then two more things, quickly, standing up.

Root 2, in two minutes. Not the write-up, the spine of it: what you assumed, what arresting the fraction with the smallest bottom number did for you, and where the contradiction landed. No notes.

Then the monsters by name, one line each: the circle everybody was counted out of, the zeros on the end of a hundred factorial, and these coins. Say what cracked each one. Then the older ones from the earlier seasons if the room asks for them, and if a name has gone, let it go. The Atlas keeps what mattered, not everything.

steps.title: The examiner flip, arc edition
steps.body:
Five problems, four seasons, and this time the grown-ups sit the paper.

Choose the five before anybody sits down. Favourites, from as many different seasons as you can manage, and at least one that beat you the first time the two of you met. Write them out or print them, one copy each, and no answers anywhere on the sheet.

Hand them out and say the rules you want. Untimed is the house rule and you should keep it. Paper is allowed. Whether they may talk to each other is your call, but decide it before they start rather than after somebody asks.

While they work, do not hover and do not rescue. Watching a grown-up be stuck is most of the point, and a hint handed over early is a problem taken away.

Then collect the papers and grade them at the whiteboard, in front of them, out loud. For each of the five: the answer, then the reason, then the thing they were most likely to be caught by. If two of them wrote different answers, say which one is right and why, kindly and without wobbling.

Last, one question you ask them, and then you stay quiet however long the quiet lasts: which of these five would you have got at ten?
checklist: I chose the five myself, from more than one season, including one that beat me the first time
They worked untimed and I did not hover, hint or rescue anybody
I graded all five at the whiteboard out loud, with the reason beside every answer
I named the trap in each problem, not just the answer
I asked which of the five they would have got at ten, and waited for the answer

steps.title: Read the ledger and the claim
steps.prompt:
Stand up with the Atlas open at the coverage ledger and both witnesses on the table, and say the claim to the room in under a minute. Entering grade 5, ready for Algebra 1, and here are the two witnesses.

Then hand the ledger to whoever in the room knows least about what you have been doing all year, and ask them to read one line of it out loud. If they cannot follow the line they just read, that line is not finished, and you rewrite it today before the Atlas closes.

steps.title: Explain it
steps.prompt:
Pick the climb on today's traverse that you actually had to fight for, and write the fight down for the Atlas. What you tried first, what that cost you, and what finally moved it. Then one line underneath naming which terrain the climb came from and what you were doing when you first met the idea.

Somebody opens this page in four years and you are not in the room to help them. Write it for that person.
